module_title: Expansion of Justice - Landmark Cases, Gram Nyayalayas, and NALSA
introduction: This advanced level explores the judicial review of tribunals, the modern legal frameworks established to provide grassroots justice (Gram Nyayalayas), and the state's constitutional obligation to provide free legal aid.

core_concepts.title: L. Chandra Kumar Case (1997)
core_concepts.description: A landmark Supreme Court judgment that declared the power of judicial review of High Courts and the Supreme Court over tribunal decisions as part of the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution. Therefore, appeals against tribunal orders can be made in the High Court.

core_concepts.title: Gram Nyayalayas Act (2008)
core_concepts.description: Established to provide access to justice at the grassroots (Panchayat) level. They act as mobile courts and have both civil and criminal jurisdiction. They are not bound by the strict Indian Evidence Act but are guided by the principles of natural justice.

core_concepts.title: National Legal Services Authority (NALSA)
core_concepts.description: Constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, to fulfill the mandate of Article 39A (DPSP - Free Legal Aid). NALSA organizes Lok Adalats and provides free legal services to the weaker sections of society.

core_concepts.title: Permanent Lok Adalat
core_concepts.description: Set up by an amendment in 2002 to deal with cases pertaining to 'Public Utility Services' (like transport, postal, telecom, power, hospital services) at the pre-litigation stage. Its awards are final and binding.

core_concepts.title: National Green Tribunal (NGT)
core_concepts.description: Established in 2010 for the effective and expeditious disposal of cases relating to environmental protection and conservation of forests. India became the third country in the world to set up a specialized environmental tribunal.

important_entities.name: Nyayadhikari
important_entities.significance: Appointed by the State Government in consultation with the High Court. They enjoy the same salary and powers as a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Appeals in criminal cases from Gram Nyayalayas do NOT go to the High Court; they go to the Court of Session. Civil appeals go to the District Court. Both must be heard and disposed of within six months.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: Direct Appeal to Supreme Court from Tribunals
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Post the L. Chandra Kumar judgment, an aggrieved party cannot directly approach the Supreme Court against the decision of a tribunal (like CAT) under Article 136. They must first go to the respective High Court.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Always link the statutory body NALSA directly to the Constitutional Directive Principle (DPSP) Article 39A (Equal justice and free legal aid).

exam_strategy_tips: In UPSC, understanding the L. Chandra Kumar case is critical for Assertion-Reasoning questions regarding the independence and judicial review of tribunals.
Pay close attention to the jurisdiction of the NGT and the specific environmental laws it is empowered to hear cases under (e.g., Wildlife Protection Act is NOT under NGT's jurisdiction).
